title: 1953 Nutts Corner Viking accident
summary: While on approach to Nutts Corner Airport at 3 miles from the runway threshold, the aircraft was 90 feet above the glideslope when it rapidly lost height and struck an approach light pole. title: 1953 Skyways Avro York disappearance
summary: On 2 February 1953, Avro York G-AHFA departed Stansted for Jamaica via Newfoundland, carrying military personnel and families including 13 children. The aircraft transmitted position reports from departure through 04:25 on 2 February. At 05:31 Gander Radio received an urgency signal followed immediately by repeated distress signals SOS, SOS, SOS DE G-A, then silence. Extensive air and sea search located oil patches and dye markers 120 miles southwest of the last reported position but no wreckage or survivors. The cause of the loss was determined to be unascertainable.
probable_cause: Cause unascertainable. Chief Investigation Officer noted possibility of uncontrollable fire in aircraft engines, but investigation concluded the loss developed suddenly and violently without determination of specific cause.

title: 1953 Avro Lincoln shootdown incident
summary: A Royal Air Force Avro Lincoln was shot down by Soviet MiG-15 fighters while conducting a training flight over East German airspace. The aircraft had intruded into the Soviet zone while flying along the agreed Hamburg-Berlin air corridor. After the aircraft was struck by cannon fire and crashed, surviving crew members who bailed out were strafed and killed by the Soviet fighters in violation of the Geneva Conventions.

title: Aeroflot 35
summary: On April 30, 1953, Aeroflot Flight 35, an Ilyushin Il-12, encountered a flock of ducks during approach to Kazan. The bird strike caused both engines to fail simultaneously. The crew successfully ditched the aircraft in the Volga River, saving 22 occupants. One passenger drowned after the successful water landing when his coat prevented him from staying afloat. The investigation found pieces of ducks between the left propeller cylinders and determined that the duck strike caused ignition failure in both engines, creating a false in-flight fire condition.

title: BOAC 783
summary: BOAC Flight 783, a de Havilland Comet jetliner registered G-ALYV, broke up in mid-air and crashed six minutes after taking off from Calcuttas Dum Dum Airport on May 2, 1953. The aircraft was climbing to 7,500 feet when radio contact was lost. Witnesses near the village of Jagalgori, approximately 25 miles northwest of Calcutta, observed the aircraft coming down in flames amid severe rain and thunderstorms. The wreckage was strewn along a five-mile track with main parts still on fire. All 43 occupants were killed.
probable_cause: Structural failure in flight caused by either severe gusts encountered in the thunderstorm, overcontrolling, or loss of control by the pilot when flying through the thundersquall. The investigators recommended consideration of structural modifications to the Comet.

title: Tachikawa air disaster
summary: A United States Air Force Douglas C-124A Globemaster II crashed on June 18, 1953, three minutes after takeoff from Tachikawa Air Base, Japan. The aircraft's No. 1 outer left engine burst into flames one minute into the flight. The commander shut down the engine and declared return to base, requesting ground-controlled approach. However, during return procedures the left wing stalled, causing the aircraft to roll left into an unrecoverable dive. The aircraft crashed into a watermelon patch 3.5 miles from the airbase, killing all 129 people aboard. The investigation determined the crash was caused by improper flap usage and airspeed loss following the port engine failure.

title: 1953 Sabena Convair Crash
summary: A Sabena Convair CV-240 crashed approximately three kilometers north of Frankfurt International Airport shortly after takeoff on October 14, 1953. The crew noticed both engines losing power shortly after liftoff and attempted to raise the flaps and maintain control, but the aircraft became uncontrollable and stalled, crashing in a wooded area near Kelsterbach. All 44 occupants perished in the wreckage fire.
probable_cause: Heavy deposit of lead on spark plugs in both engines. As the plugs warmed during takeoff, metal deposits formed a circuit that short-circuited the plugs, causing fatal engine failure and subsequent stalling and crash. It is unknown whether pilot actions contributed to the outcome or if the fatal outcome was unavoidable.
